newsitem.title: BELARUS: Russia swallows pride to maintain Belarus ties.
newsitem.headline: Russia swallows pride to maintain Belarus ties.

text.p: Moscow, humiliated by the collapse of a deal it brokered between rival factions in Belarus, will swallow its pride for a ceremony on Wednesday to mark the withdrawal to Russia of the last Soviet-era nuclear missile.

Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov is due to fly to Belarus for the ceremony, the first foreign official to visit since President Alexander Lukashenko -- ignoring international criticism -- began expanding his powers.
Rodionov will witness the removal of parts of the last of 18 missiles once deployed in the former Soviet republic, Itar-Tass news agency said, quoting a defence ministry official.

The last actual warhead was taken out on Friday, completing one of the main arms control tasks since the end of the Cold War by concentrating missiles once spread accross the Soviet Union on Russian soil.

Lukashenko, who switched the ceremony from Tuesday, has said he wanted U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry to attend as well, but Washington has shunned him since he ignored its pleas not to go ahead with a controversial referendum on Sunday.
On Tuesday Lukashenko's supporters -- boosted by the announcement of a crushing victory for the president in the referendum -- began setting up a new, breakaway parliament.

They voted down an attempt by the original parliament to impeach Lukashenko and one pro-presidential deputy, Yuri Kulikovsky, said the more than 100 breakaway deputies might take over its building by the end of the week.

While they planned to gather in the headquarters of the former communist youth league on Wednesday to continue moves to establish themselves, some 60 opposition deputies were set to reconvene in the old parliament to try to resist Lukashenko.

But they failed to muster a quorum on Tuesday and the mood among them was bitter. "We follow the power of laws. But there, they follow the law of power," Lukashenko's main rival, parliament speaker Semyon Sharetsky, told Reuters.
In a further sign of the opposition's waning power, the constitutional court on Tuesday halted the impeachment case it had brought against Lukashenko for violating the constitution.

Lukashenko had agreed in overnight crisis talks with Sharetsky and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin last week not to continue what the opposition said were unconstitutional moves to expand his powers by referendum.
But the deal broke down within hours leaving Lukashenko with a free hand and Russia, which sees Belarus as its most important strategic partner, with an awkward choice.
While western countries, whose views Russia had said it had represented during last week's mediating mission, continued their criticism of Lukashenko this week, Moscow has chosen a conciliatory path.

President Boris Yeltsin's spokesman said the Kremlin leader expected restraint from both sides in Belarus so that the situation could be resolved without violence, but Rodionov's imminent visit sent a clear message of support to Lukashenko.
